questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 1
questions.code:
a = Student("Ada", 12)
b = Student("Ben", 9)
b.credits += 3
print(a.credits, b.credits)
questions.explanation: The two calls create different objects. Changing b affects only b, so a stays at 12 while b becomes 12.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 2
questions.prompt: What must be the first parameter of this instance method?
choices: self
class
value
new
questions.explanation: Python passes the receiving object into the first parameter. The usual name is self, and the method uses it to reach that object's value.

questions.title: Trace Classes & Objects
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: `Student` is the class. Calling it creates one object, and `__init__` stores the values that belong to that object. The resulting output is 'Ada 18'.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 5
questions.prompt: In `__init__`, what is the difference between `self.name = name` and `name = name`?
choices: self.name stores it on the object; name = name only reassigns a local and is lost
They both store the value on the object
name = name raises an error
self.name creates a new class, not an attribute
questions.explanation: `self.name = name` attaches the value to the object, so other methods can read it later. `name = name` just assigns the parameter to itself, a local that vanishes when `__init__` returns, and the object never remembers the name. It runs without error but stores nothing.

questions.title: Separate objects
questions.prompt: After creating `ada = Student("Ada")` and `ben = Student("Ben")`, which statement is true?
choices: Each object has its own instance data.
The second object overwrites the first one.
Both names always point to the exact same object.
Changing `ben.name` must also change `ada.name`.
questions.explanation: Each call to a class creates a separate object unless you explicitly reuse the same object. Instance attributes belong to that particular object, so changing one student's name does not automatically change another student's name.

questions.title: When a class helps
questions.prompt: A program tracks each plant's name and also has watering behavior for that plant. What design fits?
choices: Keep every plant detail in unrelated global variables.
Use a class because the data and behavior belong together.
Use one tuple for every plant and never write helper behavior.
Use a set because plants should have no named fields.
questions.explanation: Classes are useful when several pieces of state travel with behavior that uses that state. A `Plant` object can hold a name and watering schedule while methods work with those attributes. That is clearer than scattering related values across unrelated variables.

questions.title: Constructor setup
questions.prompt: Where should a Python class usually set the starting instance attributes?
choices: Inside every method that might later need the attribute.
Only after the object is printed for the first time.
Inside `__init__`, using `self` to store values on the object.
Inside a comment above the class definition.
questions.explanation: `__init__` runs when a new object is created, so it is the natural place to set required starting attributes. Storing them on `self` makes them available to later methods on the same object. Local variables inside `__init__` disappear after the method finishes.

questions.title: Using self attributes
questions.prompt: Inside an instance method, how should code refer to a value stored on that object?
choices: Use a bare variable name and assume Python finds the object.
Use the class name for every object's personal data.
Use a global variable with the same name.
Use `self.attribute` so Python knows which object's data to read.
questions.explanation: `self` is the current object receiving the method call. Writing `self.attribute` tells Python to read or update that object's stored data. A bare name is only a local or outer variable; it is not automatically the object's attribute.

questions.title: Creating new objects
questions.prompt: What happens each time code calls a class such as `Student("Mia")`?
choices: Python creates a new object and runs `__init__` for that object.
Python edits the most recently created object instead.
Python creates only a dictionary and skips methods.
Python reuses one shared object for every student.
questions.explanation: Calling a class constructs a new instance. Python runs `__init__` to initialize that instance's attributes, then returns the object. This is why two calls to the same class can produce two independent students.

questions.title: Focused methods
questions.prompt: What makes an instance method easier to test and reuse?
choices: It changes many unrelated attributes in one call.
It focuses on one clear action for the object.
It reads user input, writes files, and updates every object at once.
It avoids `self` even though it needs object data.
questions.explanation: A focused method has a small, understandable responsibility, such as `water()` or `calculate_grade()`. That makes it easier to predict what should change after the call. Large mixed-purpose methods are harder to test because one call has too many side effects.
